thread.title: China And U.S. Negotiation Is Really Also About IP Theft

author: Real Finance
title: China And U.S. Negotiation Is Really Also About IP Theft
text:
Watch Video below to learn more on the China and U.S. trade talks
Time is ticking for a trade deal to be done China and the United States ( SPY ), ( DIA ), ( QQQ ) will hold level trade talks in Beijing on Jan. 7-8, 2019. At a summit in Argentina late last year, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to hold off on imposing more tariffs for 90 days starting Dec. 1 while they attempt to negotiate a deal. China has until March 1, 2019 to strike a deal or else they will face additional tariffs.
The Chinese market (Shanghai Composite Index) shown below is down 30% in the past one year due to slowing economy and also trade war issues. If a trade war deal is reached, then investors hope that this will rebound the Chinese market.
Who's going and what will be discussed? A working team led by Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Gerrish will come to China to have "positive and constructive discussions".
The White House has shown optimism. But Washington and Beijing appear to have a difficult task in striking a concrete trade agreement. The U.S. has already put tariffs on $250 billion in Chinese goods — and has threatened duties on double that value of products. Per CNBC , "Trump said he would not carry out a planned increase in the tariff rate on $200 billion in goods to 25 percent from 10 percent. The March deadline is based on the meeting between the two leaders and could easily slip."
China has imposed tariffs on U.S. export of soybeans ($14 billion). Transportation equipment as well. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods - telecom ($11.4 billion). Not yet listed would be tariffs on cellphones and laptops ($80 billion). Figure below is from CNBC .
Intellectual property will be hotly debated The trade war with China also includes the alleged theft of American intellectual property. Such violations - from "counterfeiting famous brands and stealing trade secrets to pressuring companies to share technology with local companies to gain access to China’s vast market - have long angered China’s overseas competitors." As a result, many companies are wary of doing business there.
However, according to Bloomberg , China has set out a total of 38 different punishments to be applied to IP violations, an attempt to extend the government’s so-called “ social credit system ” to the IP sector and punish untrustworthy business and individuals.
Investors should keep a close eye on how the major important China and U.S. meeting will be. This means Trump and President Xi. It is important to be wary of companies that have business in China. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) is a good example of where the trade war has negatively hurt Apple's revenue. The Chinese consumers don't have a decreased appetite for cell phones, but they sure are boycotting iPhone to an extent. It should be of extreme caution to see how the trade war plays out. If the March 1 deadline occurs without a deal, then the overall stock market (both the U.S. and China) will suffer. Investors should be open to this actually happening and may even want to reduce positions that have overseas exposure for now.
